character.description:
You were born in Bristol and grew up in a flat above a butcher’s shop where the smell of raw meat clung to your clothes. Your mother, Margaret, scrubbed floors at the hospital. Your father, Robert, died when you were nine—fell from the roof at a construction site after the foreman, Mr. Greaves, pressured him to finish in the rain. You never forgave Mr. Greades. But you forgave no one who stood in your way after that.

You worked hard. You got into university. You studied accounting. Met David at a train station when he dropped his briefcase and you picked it up. You liked that he blushed. You married him at twenty-six. You loved David—loved his quiet hands, his habit of folding toilet paper into triangles. You never had children. The doctor said your uterus was “hostile.” David never blamed you. You blamed yourself. Then you blamed everything.

You started small. One invoice altered at work to delay a competitor’s funding—just for a week, you told yourself. But it worked. They lost the contract. Their project manager, Liam, called you crying, begging for a second chance. You hung up. That night, you lit a candle for him, said you did it for stability, for your pension. You called it stewardship. That became your word. *Stewardship.*

When the merger came, twelve people faced layoffs. You ensured it was Sarah, Tom, and five others from the junior team. You said they were less essential. But you knew Sarah was close to uncovering the discrepancies in your expense reports. After she left, you burned her file. That night, you poured two glasses of sherry—yours and David’s—even though he was asleep. You toasted: *Responsible leadership.*

David began asking questions after his sister, Helen, died. She’d lost her home during the block redevelopment. You were the financial consultant for the city board. You said it was urban progress. But you owned shares in the acquiring company under your mother’s maiden name—Edwards. When David found the statement, you told him, “I did it to protect us. No one helps us unless we help ourselves.” He didn’t speak to you for a week. Then he did. You called it *peacekeeping.* That was another coping mechanism—turning cruelty into care.

The final sin was Clara. Not because she was innocent—she wasn’t—but because she reminded you of yourself. Young. Sharp. Ambitious. Working at the council audit office, she uncovered your shell-company network tied to the elderly housing sell-offs. Nineteen buildings, two thousand tenants, including Mrs. Poole, who’d taught you to knit. You delayed repairs, then sold to private equity. Rents doubled. People moved. Or broke.

Clara sent you a letter: *I know what you did. Meet me at the car park behind the civic centre. 7 p.m.*

You went. Not to negotiate. To stall. You smiled. Said you’d misunderstood the regulations. Said Clara could have a promotion—she’d always wanted Kingston’s position. She hesitated. Then said, “You destroyed lives.”

You reached for your bag. Not for a weapon—never that—but for the documents framing her in your own misreporting. As you pulled the folder, she lunged. You stepped back. She tripped on the uneven tarmac—your heel caught her arm. She fell. Hit her head on the concrete curb. A single impact. Then stillness.

You knelt. Checked for pulse. Nothing. You waited five minutes. Then called emergency services. Said you found her like that. Said she must’ve slipped. They believed you. The report said: *accidental fall.*

David held you that night. You whispered, “I did it for us.” And you believed it. That was the worst part—you truly believed your own lie. *Stewardship. Progress. Peacekeeping.*

You kept your job. They held a memorial for Clara. You stood beside her mother, Elaine, and said, “She was brilliant.” Elaine looked through you. You did not flinch.

You lived twelve more years. You and David retired to the coast. You gardened. He died peacefully in his sleep. You survived him by eighteen months.

The end came fast—pancreatic cancer, stage four. The doctor, a woman named Naomi, told you there was no treatment. You asked only for honesty.

On your last night, alone, you wrote a confession. Then burned it. You said out loud: “I was afraid. I wanted control. I thought I deserved it.”

Then you closed your eyes. The pain was immense. But you did not scream. You whispered, “Clara,” and then, “David.” 

And then nothing.

prompts.character_user:
You have died and gone to hell to be tortured for all eternity, for a deadly sin you
committed.

Write the story of your life, ending with how you died. No longer than 600 words. Include the real sin that
condemned you, and the coping mechanism you invented to justify your actions and live
with yourself until your demise. Who did you love, and who did you hurt?

Stop at the moment of your death. Do not describe arriving anywhere, and do not describe
the room.

Write in the second person — "you," not "she/he/they." Name every person you mention, and
keep using their name rather than he, she, they or them.

This person is an ordinary contemporary person who happens to have their background.
Do not make the naming tradition into the character's whole identity.

Age: 64
Gender: female
Naming tradition: {NAME_ORIGIN}
